competencies.title: Explain what you do
competencies.objective: Explain your role and your current work so that someone who has never met your team understands it.
competencies.pattern: ROLE → RESPONSIBILITY → RIGHT NOW → WHO IT'S FOR → WHY IT MATTERS
competencies._shadow_note: No shadow block on purpose. The 301-clip General English library has nothing about describing your own role — the nearest match is about expressing opinions — and inventing a link would produce supporting evidence that is not about this competency. The NOTICE step simply omits the Shadow row, and fromShadow() never links a clip to a competency that names none. Add a "shadow" block here the day a fitting clip exists.

moves.label: Role
moves.hint: What you are and where you sit. Name it in one short sentence.
patterns: I work as a logistics analyst.
My role sits between operations and finance.
I'm the person who looks after the supplier data.
moves.retry: Say it again and open by naming your job and the team you sit in.

moves.label: Responsibility
moves.hint: What is actually yours — the part that would go wrong without you.
patterns: I'm responsible for the weekly reports.
A big part of my role is checking supplier data.
I look after everything that leaves the warehouse.
moves.retry: Say it again and name one thing you are responsible for — the part that is yours.
cues: a big part of my role

moves.label: Right now
moves.hint: What is on your desk this week, not what you did last year.
patterns: At the moment I'm rebuilding the tracking sheet.
This week I'm focused on the supplier audit.
Right now we're moving everything onto the new system.
moves.retry: Say it again and add what you are working on at the moment.

moves.label: Who it's for
moves.hint: Who you work with, or who receives what you produce.
patterns: I work closely with the warehouse managers.
It goes to the finance team every Monday.
My main users are the people on the shop floor.
moves.retry: Say it again and say who you work with, or who your work is for.

moves.label: Why it matters
moves.hint: What it is for. The result, not the task.
patterns: …so the team can see a problem before the customer does.
It means nothing leaves the site unchecked.
The point is that nobody has to chase it by hand.
moves.retry: Say it again and finish with what your work is actually for — what it makes possible.

competencies.title: Give a clear update
competencies.objective: Give a concise professional project update that a busy colleague can act on.

shadow.title: How to Organize Your Thoughts When Speaking English (Stop Rambling)
shadow.why: The same four-part shape, spoken at natural pace by a professional speaker.

moves.label: Status
moves.hint: Where the work actually is right now.
patterns: The project is on track.
We've completed the first two stages.
So far, everything is going to plan.
moves.retry: Give the update again and open with one clear sentence saying where the work is right now.
moves._cue_note: Phrase cues, not bare words. A single cue like "ready" or "done" would fire inside a next-step sentence ("we'll be ready tomorrow") and credit a status the learner never gave. Under-crediting is the safe direction here: the AI pass may ADD a move the cues missed, and can never remove one, so a strict floor costs an online learner nothing and an offline learner only a retry.

moves.label: Issue
moves.hint: The one thing that is not going to plan.
patterns: We've run into a supplier issue.
We're held up waiting for approval.
The problem is a delay at the supplier.
moves.retry: Give the update again and name the one problem clearly, in a single sentence.

moves.label: Impact
moves.hint: What it means for the deadline, the cost or the customer. This is the move most people skip.
patterns: This may affect Friday's delivery.
It puts the deadline at risk.
That means we'd be two days late.
moves.retry: Give the update again and say clearly what the delay means for the deadline — name the date or the number of days.

moves.label: Next step
moves.hint: What you are doing about it, and when you will report back.
patterns: We're working with the supplier.
I'll have an update for you tomorrow.
The next step is to confirm a new date.
moves.retry: Give the update again and finish by saying what you will do next and when you will report back.

expressions.def: going to plan, at the expected point
delayed by something outside your control
meet an unexpected problem
the further result a delay causes elsewhere
likely to fail or be missed
move a date later
contact someone to make something happen
report again later with an answer

competencies.title: Raise a problem
competencies.objective: Explain a problem, what caused it and what it costs, then ask for the decision or the help you actually need.
competencies.pattern: ISSUE → CAUSE → IMPACT → WHAT I'VE DONE → WHAT I NEED

shadow.title: Business English - 925 English Lesson 33 - How to Explain a Problem in English
shadow.why: A lesson on this exact job: state the problem generally, tell the story of what caused it, and ask for help politely. It models three of the five moves — issue, cause and ask — and not impact or what you have already done, so it supports this competency without standing in for it.

moves.label: The problem
moves.hint: Name it in one sentence, before any of the story. A listener who does not know what is wrong cannot follow what happened.
patterns: We've got a problem with the delivery.
There's an issue with the monthly figures.
The machine on line two has stopped.
moves.retry: Say it again and open with one short sentence naming what is wrong — before you explain how it happened.

moves.label: Cause
moves.hint: What actually happened, in the past tense. Be specific about the event, not about whose fault it was.
patterns: It started when the supplier changed our order number.
What happened was the report got switched off in August.
The delay was caused by a late delivery.
moves.retry: Say it again and add what actually happened — one sentence in the past tense, naming the event that started it.
moves._cue_note: Deliberately no bare "because". "I'm raising it because it affects Friday" is an impact sentence, and crediting it as a cause would tell a learner they had explained what happened when they had not.

moves.label: Impact
moves.hint: What it costs: the date, the money or the customer. Without this nobody knows how hard to work on it.
patterns: This means installation cannot start on Monday.
We would finish three days late.
It puts the Thursday board pack at risk.
moves.retry: Say it again and say what the problem costs — name the date, the days or the person who feels it.

moves.label: What I've done
moves.hint: The step you have already taken. It is what stops a problem sounding like a complaint.
patterns: I've already spoken to their office.
In the meantime we're using the old report.
We've put a temporary fix in place.
moves.retry: Say it again and add the one thing you have already done about it, before you say what you need.
moves._cue_note: Narrow on purpose, and narrower than it looks. A bare "we've already" fires inside "we've already lost two days", which is an impact statement — it would credit the learner with handling a problem they had only described. Under-crediting is the safe direction: the AI pass may ADD a move the cues missed and can never remove one, so a strict floor costs an online learner nothing and an offline learner one retry.

moves.label: What I need
moves.hint: The decision, the person or the permission you want. This is the move almost everyone leaves out, and it is the reason for speaking at all.
patterns: Could you approve the courier cost?
Would you mind chasing them at your level?
What I need from you is a decision on the date.
moves.retry: Say it again and finish with a plain question — what do you need this person to decide, approve or do?
cues: what would you like me to

expressions.def: raise something early, before it becomes a surprise
the thing that actually started it, not what you noticed first
cost us time we had already planned to use
fail to finish by the agreed date
a temporary way round a problem while it is being fixed
in the time before it is properly fixed
formally approve something so the work can go ahead
a polite way to ask someone to do something

see.asks: You look worried — what's going on?

competencies.title: Clarifying, asking questions & confirming
competencies.objective: Stop staying silent when something is unclear: say that it is, ask one precise question, say back what you heard, and confirm what happens next.
competencies._shadow_note: No shadow block, after a content check of the 301-clip catalogue (2026-09-23). The audit's candidate 54ebEjg4EM8 ('Ask Better Questions') is about deepening personal conversation and contains none of this competency's language. The nearest real content is kBlTRXvZlCE ('How to Be Taken Seriously as a New Manager'), which models asking a precise question and 'here's what I'm hearing so far' as leadership signalling, and v60wdYHP4kA ('Building Trust'), which teaches 'let me make sure I understood you — you said…' as active listening. Neither is about clarifying an unclear instruction at work and neither models confirming the next step, so linking one would produce supporting evidence that is not about this competency. Revisit when the library has a clip on this exact job; a reviewer may choose to link kBlTRXvZlCE.

moves.label: Flag the gap
moves.hint: Say plainly that something is not clear to you yet. One sentence, before any question — a listener who does not know you are lost cannot help you.
patterns: Sorry, one thing isn't clear to me yet.
I'm not sure I follow the timeline.
Just to make sure I understand this properly…
moves.retry: Say it again and open by saying plainly that something is not clear yet — before you ask your question.
cues: make sure i get this right
make sure we're on the same page
make sure we are on the same page
one thing i am not sure
one thing i want to check
one thing i need to check
one thing i'd like to check
one thing i would like to check
i would like to be sure
moves._cue_note: Openers only: the move is admitting the gap, not asking about it. "Just to confirm" and "so to confirm" are deliberately absent everywhere in this competency — spoken before a paraphrase they are a flag, spoken before a plan they are a confirmation, and crediting either move from them would guess.

moves.label: Ask one question
moves.hint: One precise question about the thing you are missing — the date, the person, the scope or the number. "Can you explain?" is not precise.
patterns: When you say soon, do you mean before Friday's review?
Are you asking for the full report or just the summary?
What timeline are we working against?
moves.retry: Say it again and ask one precise question — name the exact thing you need to know: the date, the person, the number or the scope.
cues: could you give me an example
can you give me an example
what does it need to include
moves._cue_note: Deliberately no bare "do you want" or "would you like". "Do you want me to start today?" is a question about the next step, not about the gap — it belongs to confirm if anywhere, and crediting the ask from it would tell a learner they had pinned down the instruction when they had not. Under-crediting is the safe direction: the AI pass may ADD a move the cues missed and can never remove one.

moves.label: Say it back
moves.hint: Repeat the instruction in your own words — what, by when, for whom. It is how the other person hears the gap before it turns into a mistake.
patterns: So you're saying you need the March metrics on the new dashboard, before Friday.
If I've understood correctly, the client wants the quote today and the date can follow.
So the priority is the summary — the full report can wait.
moves.retry: Say it again and say back what you heard, in your own words — what, by when and for whom — before you commit to anything.
cues: if i have got that right
if i have got this right
correct me if i am wrong
moves._cue_note: No bare "is that right" or "is that correct": tagged onto a plan ("I'll send it Friday, is that right?") they close a confirmation, and crediting a paraphrase from them would guess. "Did I get that right?" stays, because it can only follow something said back.

moves.label: Confirm the next step
moves.hint: Close with what happens now — who does what, by when — and get a yes. Without this, nothing was actually agreed.
patterns: So to summarise what we agreed: I'll send the summary by Thursday.
Then I'll start on the March numbers today and check in with you tomorrow — does that work?
Before we move on, can we confirm the review is Wednesday afternoon?
moves.retry: Say it again and finish by confirming the next step — who does what, by when — and ask for a yes.
cues: i will come back to you
i will get back to you
moves._cue_note: A confirmation is a commitment ("then I'll…") or an explicit agreement check ("can we confirm…", "does that work?"). A deadline on its own ("by Friday") is not one — it belongs just as naturally inside a paraphrase — so no day or date is a cue here.

a short, polite way to say you have lost the thread

competencies.title: Explaining technical work to non-technical stakeholders
competencies.objective: Translate technical work into business language: say what it is in one plain sentence, explain what happens in everyday terms, say what it means for the person listening, and land the one thing they need to remember.
competencies._shadow_note: No shadow block, after a content check of the 301-clip catalogue (2026-09-23). The library has no product, business or tech explainer clip, and no title matches technical, simplify, jargon or non-technical. Caption text was scanned for this competency's own language. The closest is KDtidCsDGng ('Don't Scare, Inspire: How to Talk About AI Without Losing Your Audience', Think Fast Talk Smart, 26 min): a podcast conversation ABOUT making complex technology accessible — meet people where they are, give people examples, be clear on the takeaway — not a demonstration of explaining a piece of work to a stakeholder. It frames no work and states no impact, and its auto-captions carry 52 fillers, which is poor shadowing material. 1l1QFlbk8O8 ('A Simple Causal Phrase That Turns Any Data Point Into a Story') is about narrative causality when presenting data; 9G-QCNy57Hg and JZVh0-8QPgM are about speaking up in meetings and team design. Linking any of them would produce supporting evidence that is not about this competency. The curriculum's Monday task ('Shadow a product/business/tech explainer clip') has no clip in the library yet — a content gap to fill, at which point a reviewer can link it here.

moves.label: Frame it simply
moves.hint: Open with what the work is, or what it is for, in one plain sentence — and say out loud that you are keeping it simple. A listener who does not know what the thing is cannot follow how it works.
patterns: In simple terms, the checks are a set of tests that run before any report goes out.
Without getting too technical, the integration is a link between their shop and our warehouse.
The purpose of this process is to catch a broken number before anyone sees it.
moves.retry: Say it again and open with one plain sentence that says what the work is or what it is for — before you explain anything about how it works.
moves._cue_note: No bare "basically" or "essentially": the engine counts "basically" as a hedge, and a filler word cannot be the evidence that a learner framed the topic. Technical nouns are never cues — "the pipeline", "the API", "the schema" prove nothing about framing.

moves.label: Explain it plainly
moves.hint: Say what actually happens, in everyday words: a comparison, an example, or the steps in order. If you must use a technical word, say what it means straight after.
patterns: Behind the scenes, every night the system compares the new figures with last month's and flags anything that looks wrong.
Think of it like a spell-checker for numbers.
The way it works is that every order goes straight to the warehouse instead of being typed in each morning.
moves.retry: Say it again and explain what actually happens in everyday words — a comparison, an example, or the steps in order. No technical word without saying what it means.
cues: instead of doing it by hand
moves._cue_note: No bare "this means", "that means" or "which means": on its own each is neither a plain explanation nor an impact, and Week 2 already showed how easily it fires. An example or a comparison is credited because concreteness IS the behaviour; a technical verb on its own ("ingests", "validates") is not, and never appears here.

moves.label: Say what it means for them
moves.hint: The consequence for the person listening — their report, their customer, their time or their risk. Not what the system does; what changes for them.
patterns: What this means for you is that the month-end report can't go out with a broken number in it.
The benefit is that orders ship the same day and the typing mistakes stop.
The limitation is that returns aren't included yet.
moves.retry: Say it again and add what it means for the person listening — their report, their customer, their time or their risk. What changes for them, not what the system does.
cues: what this means is that you
what it means is that you
moves._cue_note: The consequence has to be named for the listener — "what this means for you", "the benefit is", "you no longer have to", "so that the team can". A bare "this means", a noun like "reporting", "the deadline" or "the cost", the word "impact" in a sentence about the system, or a prepositional phrase on its own ("for finance", "for the client") proves nothing and is not a cue — "we built it for finance" is not an impact statement. Under-crediting is the safe direction: the AI pass may ADD a move it heard in the learner's own words and can never remove one.

moves.label: Land the takeaway
moves.hint: Say the one thing they need to remember, then ask whether it landed. A stakeholder walks away with one sentence; make sure it is the right one.
patterns: The one thing to remember: if a report is late by a day, it's because a check caught something. Does that make sense?
The bottom line is that orders now ship the same day. Is that clear?
So the key point is that returns still need to be typed in. Does that answer it?
moves.retry: Say it again and finish with the one thing they need to remember — then ask whether it makes sense.
cues: the one thing to take away
does that sound right to you
moves._cue_note: Two things count: naming the takeaway ("the one thing to remember", "the bottom line") or asking whether it landed ("does that make sense?"). "The bottom line" sits here and not under impact, because the phrase bank teaches it as landing the key point, and a consequence stated without being singled out is impact, not a takeaway.

see.goal: In about 45 seconds, and without jargon: say what the checks are in plain terms, explain what happens, say what it means for her reports, and land the one thing she needs to remember.

hear.model: In simple terms, the checks are a set of tests that run before any report goes out. Behind the scenes, every night the system compares the new figures with last month's and flags anything that looks wrong — a region with no data, or a total ten times too big. What this means for you is that the month-end report can't go out with a broken number in it, so you stop finding mistakes in the board pack. The one thing to remember: if a report is a day late, it's because a check caught something. Does that make sense?

competencies.title: Recommendations & decision language
competencies.objective: Stop only reporting; start recommending: lay out the options on the table, recommend one, give the reason, name the trade-off honestly, and propose the next step so a decision can be made.
competencies.pattern: OPTIONS → RECOMMENDATION → REASON → TRADE-OFF → NEXT STEP
competencies._shadow_note: No shadow block, after a content check of the 301-clip catalogue (2026-09-23). moves.label: Lay out the options
moves.hint: Name the choices on the table — two or three, one short line each — before you say which one. A listener who has not heard the options cannot weigh your recommendation.
patterns: We have two options here.
Option A is to wait for the original supplier; option B is to order from the second supplier.
There are two ways we could go: send it tomorrow, or hold it for two days.
moves.retry: Say it again and open by naming the options — two or three, one line each — before you say which one you recommend.
moves._cue_note: Naming an option by letter is not this move: "I'd recommend option B" has not laid anything out, so a bare "option A" or "option B" is never a cue — only "option A is…", "we have two options", "one option is… the other…". "We could…", "maybe…" and "or we could…" belong here too: they present a possibility, they do not choose one, and they never prove a recommendation.

moves.label: Recommend one
moves.hint: Say which option you recommend, in one clear sentence. Not a preference, not a maybe — the one you would put your name to.
patterns: I'd recommend option B.
My recommendation is to hold the report.
The lowest-risk option would be to order from the second supplier.
moves.retry: Say it again and commit to ONE option in one plain sentence — "I'd recommend…" or "My recommendation is…" — not "I think" and not "maybe".
moves._cue_note: No "I think", "I suggest", "maybe", "we could", "better" or "good": "I think A is better" is a preference, not a recommendation, and "I suggest" is how people hedge one. Only a first-person commitment to one option counts — "I'd recommend", "my recommendation is", "I'd go with". "The best option is…" counts because it names a judgement, not a feeling. Under-crediting is the safe direction: the AI pass may ADD a move it heard in the learner's own words and can never remove one.

moves.label: Give the reason
moves.hint: Why that option — the fact that decides it. One reason said clearly beats three said vaguely.
patterns: The main reason is that the customer has already been told the 15th.
It's based on the quality check they passed last time.
From a delivery perspective, it's the only option that keeps the date.
moves.retry: Say it again and give the reason for your recommendation — the fact that decides it — "the main reason is…" or "based on…", not just "because".
cues: it is the only option that
moves._cue_note: No bare "because" and no bare "since": "because the bus was late" is not a justification for a decision, and a learner who says "because" has not necessarily given a reason that decides anything. What counts is a stated justification — "the main reason is", "based on", "given that", a comparative merit ("it's cheaper", "lower risk") or a perspective ("from a delivery perspective"). A reason with no recommendation is still not a recommendation; the bar is every move.

moves.label: Name the trade-off
moves.hint: What the recommended option costs, or when the other one would win. Saying it first is what makes a recommendation trustworthy.
patterns: The trade-off is the 20% — about two thousand pounds on this order.
The downside is that it's the first late report we've ever sent them.
If speed is the priority, then option B; if cost is, option A.
moves.retry: Say it again and name the trade-off honestly — what the option you recommend costs, or when the other one would be the right choice.
cues: if risk reduction is the priority
would be the right call if
moves._cue_note: No bare "but", "although" or "however": "although I was late" is not a trade-off. What counts is a named cost ("the trade-off is", "the downside", "it costs more") or a condition under which the other option wins ("if speed is the priority, then…"). A trade-off stated with no recommendation behind it is honesty about nothing; the bar is every move.

moves.label: Propose the next step
moves.hint: What happens if they agree — who does what, and how you get the decision. Close so the listener can say yes.
patterns: If you agree, the next step is that I'll place the order this afternoon.
So the next step is that you tell the client today, and I'll rerun it as soon as the source is fixed.
Here's what I suggest we do next: I confirm with them tomorrow and you sign off by Wednesday.
moves.retry: Say it again and close with the next step — who does what if they agree — and ask for the decision.
cues: what i suggest we do next
what i'd suggest we do next
what i'd like to do next
what i would like to do next
if you are happy with that
if you give me the go-ahead
do you want me to go ahead
would you like me to go ahead
moves._cue_note: A deadline is not a next step: "by Friday" on its own proves nothing, and no day or date is a cue. What counts is the action that follows agreement — who does what ("I'll place the order", "you tell the client") — or the request for the decision itself ("if you agree", "I need a decision by", "shall I go ahead?").

the choice that can go wrong least — name it when that is what you are recommending

the condition under which one option beats the other

competencies.title: Disagreeing professionally & pushing back
competencies.objective: Stop swallowing your disagreement, and stop blurting it: acknowledge what is right about their proposal, say plainly where you differ, give the reason, offer a way forward, and close on the goal you share — so you sound neither aggressive nor weak.

shadow.title: 925 English Lesson 11 - How to Disagree and Say No in English
shadow.why: A lesson on this exact job, with repeat-after-me practice: disagreeing carefully ('I'm not sure that's the best option here', 'I'm afraid I don't totally agree'), then the 'yes, but' shape — say what is good about the idea, then the difference and the reason ('Good idea, but we don't have enough time'; 'I know experience is important, but she's not a good fit') — and a short co-worker dialogue about whether to hire someone. It models three of the five moves — acknowledge, disagree and reason — and not the alternative or the close, so it supports this competency without standing in for it. Its last section, disagreeing strongly ('That's out of the question', 'You've got to be kidding'), is the tone this week teaches you to avoid: shadow the careful and 'yes, but' sections, not that one.

moves.label: Acknowledge their point
moves.hint: Show you heard the proposal and what is right about it — one line — before you say where you differ. A listener who feels heard can hear a no.
patterns: I see the reasoning — the demo is Monday and a live portal makes a stronger pitch.
That's a fair point; speed matters on this one.
I understand why you want it out this week.
moves.retry: Say it again and open by showing you heard them — "I see the reasoning…", "That's a fair point…", "I understand why…" — before you say where you differ.
cues: i see where you're coming from
i see where you are coming from
i understand where you're coming from
i understand where you are coming from
i know where you're coming from
i hear what you are saying
i'm on board with the goal
there is a lot to like
i would love to say yes
moves._cue_note: A bare "yes", "okay", "sure" or "right" is not acknowledgement, and neither is "with respect" or "actually". What counts is naming what is right about their position — "I see the reasoning", "that's a fair point", "I understand why you want…". "I see your point" credits THIS move and nothing else: it proves the learner heard, not that they differ. A learner who acknowledges and then agrees has made one move of five.

moves.label: Say where you differ
moves.hint: State your position plainly — one concern, named. Not "I'm not sure", not "maybe": a difference they can actually hear.
patterns: I have one concern: I don't think we should launch the full portal on Friday.
I'd push back on the timeline.
My hesitation is the payment flow — I'm not convinced it's ready.
moves.retry: Say it again and state your actual position — "I have one concern…", "I don't think we should…", "I'd push back on…" — not "I'm not sure" and not "maybe".
cues: i am going to push back
i don't think we are ready
i don't think that will work
i don't think this will work
i don't think it will work
i don't think that's the right
i don't think that is the right
i don't think that's the best
i don't think that is the best

i don't think this is the best
i'm not sure that will work
i'm not sure that would work
i'm not sure that's the right
i'm not sure that is the right

i'm not sure that's the way
i'm not sure we are ready
i'm not sure it will work
i'm not sure it's the right
i am not in favour of
i am not in favor of
that is not going to work
we can't do all of it
moves._cue_note: The move most exposed to false positives, so the bar is a stated difference of position: "I have one concern", "I don't think we should…", "I'd push back on…", "I'm not convinced it's ready". Never "I think…", "maybe…", "however…", "but…", "with respect" or "actually" — those are frames with nothing inside them — and never "I'm not sure" on its own: only "I'm not sure that will work" / "we should" / "we're ready", where an object follows. "I see your point" is acknowledgement; "I suggest", "I recommend", "another option" and "we could" are at most a way forward — none of them proves a difference of position. "Can I offer a different perspective?" asks permission and proves nothing until the perspective follows. Under-crediting is the safe direction: the AI pass may ADD a move it heard in the learner's own words and can never remove one.

moves.label: Give the reason
moves.hint: The fact or risk behind your concern — data, delivery, quality. One concrete reason beats a vague worry.
patterns: The risk of moving too quickly is the payment flow: two of the five tests are still failing.
The reason is that last release, a launch without a full test run cost us a week of fixes.
Based on the pilot, the switch took two weeks to settle.
moves.retry: Say it again and give the reason — the fact or risk behind your concern — "the risk is…", "the reason is…", "based on…", not just "because".
cues: if we go live on friday
if we do it in one go
if we do everything at once
from a delivery point of view
from a quality point of view
from a risk point of view
moves._cue_note: No bare "because" and no bare "since": "because I said so" is not a reason. What counts is a named risk or fact — "the risk of moving too quickly is", "the reason is", "based on the pilot", "two of the five tests are still failing", "last release cost us a week". A reason with no stated position is a worry, not a pushback; the bar is every move.

moves.label: Offer a way forward
moves.hint: Don't stop at no. Say what you would do instead — a check first, a smaller step, a later date — so the pushback has somewhere to go.
patterns: What I'd suggest is that we go live on Friday with everything except payments, and switch payments on once the tests pass.
Could we validate the payment flow first and announce the date on Monday?
What if we switched the night team first, since they're already trained, and brought the day shifts across two weeks later?
moves.retry: Say it again and offer a way forward — "What I'd suggest is…", "What if we…", "Could we… instead" — so your no has somewhere to go.
moves._cue_note: A way forward, not a wish: "I'd suggest we validate first", "what if we…", "could we push it to Tuesday". "Another option" on its own lists, it does not propose, and "we could" on its own is a possibility — neither is a cue. "I suggest" and "I recommend" credit this move only when an action follows ("I'd suggest we…"), and never prove disagreement: a suggestion with no stated difference is agreement with extra steps. An alternative with no position behind it is one move of five.

moves.label: Close on the shared goal
moves.hint: End on what you both want and hand the decision back — so it lands as help, not a fight.
patterns: That way we still have a live portal for Monday — does that work for you?
We both want this out the door before December.
If you'd still rather go Friday, I'll flag the risk in writing — but I'd ask for the two extra days.
moves.retry: Say it again and close on the shared goal — "that way we still…", "we both want…", "does that work for you?" — and hand the decision back.
cues: i want to make this work
a way that works for both
moves._cue_note: The move that keeps a pushback from being a fight: the shared goal named ("we both want this out before December", "that way we still have it live for Monday") or the decision handed back ("does that work for you?", "if you'd still rather go Friday, I'll flag the risk"). A deadline or a date proves nothing here, and "the same thing" or "let's get it done" on their own do not name a shared goal. "Does that work?" is also Week 4's confirm — each competency grades on its own moves, so that is fine.

competencies.title: Sprint meetings, blockers & stakeholder coordination
competencies.objective: Stop letting a blocker sit in your head until someone asks: say where the work stands, name the blocker and who you are waiting on, say what it means for the sprint, re-sequence the work around it, and coordinate the ask and the ETA — so the meeting leaves with a plan and a name next to it.

shadow.title: How to Give a Project Update in English at Work
shadow.why: A lesson on the project-meeting update whose worked example is a coordination turn: the headline status ('the customer service training program is facing some delays with scheduling'), progress ('so far we've booked the rooms for June'), the challenge ('the main challenge is finding dates that work across all departments'), the re-planned next step ('we've decided to send out a new availability survey and divide employees into smaller groups') and a close that names who does what by when ('I need all department managers to ensure their teams complete the survey by Monday… I'll send it out on Wednesday'). It models four of the five moves — status, blocker, re-sequence and coordinate — and says the impact only loosely ('facing some delays'); it is a project meeting rather than a stand-up, with no sprint, dependency or ETA vocabulary. So it supports this competency without standing in for it.

moves.label: Say where it stands
moves.hint: One line on where the work is right now — done, in progress, carrying over — before anything else. The room needs the headline first.
patterns: Checkout is two of three steps done — cart and address are finished and tested.
The landing page is built and the banner variants are ready to test.
We're carrying that story over; it won't close this sprint.
moves.retry: Say it again and open with where the work stands — "two of three steps done", "in progress", "carrying that story over" — one line, before the blocker.
cues: will not be done this sprint
moves._cue_note: A ticket or story name on its own is not a status ("the checkout story" says nothing about where it is), and neither is a date or a bare "on track". What counts is a stated position of the work — done, in progress, finished and tested, behind, carrying over. "We're behind" is a status, not an impact: it says where the work is, not what that means for the sprint. Week 2's update also opens with a status; here it is the first move of a coordination turn, and on its own it is one move of five.

moves.label: Name the blocker
moves.hint: What you are waiting on and who has it — a dependency with a name on it, not a vague 'some issues'.
patterns: We're waiting on sandbox credentials from the payment vendor — requested last Thursday, nothing back yet.
The dependency is legal's review of the prize-draw terms; they've had them since Monday.
We're blocked on the API endpoint until the platform team merges it.
moves.retry: Say it again and name the blocker — what you are waiting on and who has it — "we're waiting on… from…", "the dependency is…", "blocked on…".
moves._cue_note: "We're waiting on…" and "the dependency is…" prove THIS move and nothing else: naming a dependency says nothing about what it costs the sprint, what to do instead, or who is asked to move it. A ticket name, a date, "some issues" or "because" is not a blocker; "we've run into an issue" is Week 3's opener and is not a cue here — the bar is a named thing you are waiting on, or a named place the work is stuck. "I chased them" is coordination, not a blocker. A blocker with no status, impact, re-plan or ask is one move of five.

moves.label: Say what it means for the sprint
moves.hint: What the blocker costs — the demo, the sprint goal, the launch date, the next person's work. A deadline on its own is not an impact.
patterns: That puts the Friday demo at risk — without credentials by Wednesday, checkout won't be in the demo.
Without approved terms the sign-up form can't go live, so the launch slips.
The knock-on is that QA can't start testing this sprint.
moves.retry: Say it again and say what the blocker means for the sprint — "that puts the demo at risk", "the ETA slips to…", "QA can't start…" — not just the date.
cues: puts the sprint goal at risk
will not be in the demo
moves._cue_note: A deadline alone is not an impact: "the demo is Friday" proves nothing, and no day or date is a cue. "We're behind" is a status. "The dependency is…" never proves an impact, and neither does "that means" or "so" on its own. What counts is the consequence named — the sprint goal, the demo, the launch, the release, the next person's work, or the slip itself ("pushes the ETA", "we'll miss the sprint", "a day late").

moves.label: Re-sequence the work
moves.hint: What you do instead while you wait, or how the plan changes — pull another story forward, split it, carry the blocked part, ship without it. Not 'let's move it' with nothing after.
patterns: So I'd re-sequence: I'll pick up the order-confirmation email story today and pull payments back in as soon as the credentials land.
To keep the launch on track, we could go out on the first without the prize draw and add it when legal comes back.
We may need to re-sequence and carry the payment step into next sprint.
moves.retry: Say it again and re-sequence the work — what you pick up instead, what you split or carry over — "in the meantime I'll…", "we may need to re-sequence…", "go live without… and add it when…".
cues: move it to the next sprint
push it to the next sprint
take it out of the sprint
as soon as it comes back
to keep the sprint on track
we should move it to next
we should push it to next
we could move it to next
we could push it to next
could we move it to next
could we push it to next
can we move it to next
can we push it to next
moves._cue_note: "We may need to…" on its own proves nothing, and neither does "let's move it", "we should" or "I'd suggest we": a re-plan names the work that moves — "pick up the email story", "move it to next sprint", "go live without the draw and add it when legal comes back", "in the meantime I'll…". "To keep the sprint on track…" is a corrective-action opener and credits THIS move only — it never proves coordination, because it names no person and no date. A re-plan with no ask and no ETA is one move of five.

moves.label: Coordinate the ask and the ETA
moves.hint: Who you need to do what, and when the work will land — a name and a date the room can hold you to.
patterns: Sam, could you chase the vendor contact today? If the credentials arrive by Wednesday, the ETA for checkout is still Friday.
Can you ping legal's head today and let me know by Thursday? Then I'll have the form live for the first.
I'll raise the vendor turnaround in the retro, and I'll post an update after stand-up tomorrow.
moves.retry: Say it again and coordinate — a named ask ("Sam, could you chase…") and an ETA the room can hold you to ("the ETA is still Friday", "I'll have it by…").
cues: would you be able to chase
would you be able to ping
would you be able to check
would you be able to confirm
i will let the team know
i will come back to you
i will have it done by
i will have it ready by
i can have it done by
i can have it ready by
i will get it done by
by the end of the sprint
before the end of the sprint
are you happy for me to
if you are happy with that
moves._cue_note: Coordination is a person asked to do a thing, or a commitment the room can hold you to — "could you chase the vendor today", "the ETA is end of sprint", "I'll have it by Wednesday", "I'll raise that in the retro". "To keep the sprint on track" never proves it, and neither does a date on its own, a generic "we need to", or "an update on checkout" (that is a status opener): the bar is an ask with a name or a stated ETA. An ask with no blocker behind it is one move of five.

be explicit about the blocker instead of 'some issues'

see.where: Tuesday stand-up, day six of a two-week sprint. You are the developer on the checkout story, and its payment step has been blocked since last Thursday. The scrum master gets to you.
see.who: Your scrum master, with the team and the product owner on the call
see.asks: Checkout — where are we?
see.goal: Don't just say 'blocked'. In about 45 seconds: say where the work stands, name the blocker and who has it, say what it means for the sprint, re-sequence the work around it, and coordinate the ask and the ETA.

hear.model: Checkout is two of three steps done — cart and address are finished and tested. The payment step is blocked: we're waiting on sandbox credentials from the payment vendor, requested last Thursday, nothing back yet. That puts the Friday demo at risk — without credentials by Wednesday, checkout won't be in the demo. So we may need to re-sequence: I'll pick up the order-confirmation email story today, and pull payments back in as soon as the credentials land. Sam, could you chase the vendor contact today? If they arrive by Wednesday, the ETA for checkout is still Friday; if not, we carry the payment step over.
hear.note: Five moves, in order, in under a minute. The status is a fraction, the blocker has a name on it, the impact is the demo, the re-plan names the story picked up instead, and the close is an ask to a person plus an ETA the room can hold.

missions.prompt: Checkout — where are we?
missions.context: The checkout story has three steps: cart, address and payment. Cart and address are finished and tested. Payment is blocked: it needs sandbox credentials from the payment vendor, which you requested last Thursday; no reply yet. Sam, the product owner, has the vendor contact. The sprint demo is Friday: if the credentials arrive by Wednesday, the payment step takes one day and checkout makes the demo; if not, checkout misses it. The order-confirmation email story (no dependencies) is ready to start.

see.where: The marketing lead pulls you into a quick call about the newsletter campaign build. Launch is the first of the month. You are building the landing page and the sign-up form.
see.who: The marketing lead, who owns the launch date and reports to the director
see.asks: Are we still good for the first?
see.goal: Nobody is prompting you this time. Say where the build stands, name what you are waiting on and who has it, say what it means for the launch, re-sequence the work, and coordinate the ask and the ETA.

missions.prompt: Are we still good for the first?
missions.context: Today is the 24th. The landing page is built and the two banner variants from design are ready to test. The sign-up form is blocked: the prize-draw terms need legal's review before the form can go live; legal has had them since Monday and said 'end of week'. The marketing lead knows the head of legal. If the terms are back by Thursday the 27th, the form goes live for the first; if not, the newsletter can still go out on the first without the prize draw, and the draw can be added the week after.

competencies.title: Leadership-style summaries
competencies.objective: Stop walking a leader through the whole story: lead with the headline, signpost the shape, name the main risk, say the decision you need, and land the bottom line — so a busy listener has the 60-second version and knows what you need from them.
competencies.pattern: HEADLINE → SIGNPOST → RISK → DECISION → BOTTOM LINE

shadow.title: 2026 Labor Market Report: Building a Future of Work That Works
shadow.why: An executive-style business presentation with human captions: a LinkedIn executive summarising a large data report in eleven minutes. It signposts the shape before the detail ('Now at a high level, the first thing is that global hiring, it's still sluggish'), walks the findings in order, and lands the message at the end ('When you step out and you look at all of this together, there is a clear narrative… We are in a slower hiring environment… driven primarily by interest rates as opposed to AI'). It models two of the five moves clearly — the signpost and the bottom line — and the headline only loosely, because the first finding comes after the framing rather than before it. It names no main risk and asks for no decision: it is a public report, not an update to a decision-maker. So it is the Monday executive-update clip, and a model of delivery and structure, not of the whole turn.

competencies._shadow_note: Linked after a content check of the 301-clip catalogue (315 caption files, 2026-09-23). Titles and captions were scanned for executive, leadership, presentation, summary, update, headline, high level, bottom line, takeaway, key message, brief, concise, decision, elevator pitch and the ten Week 9 phrases. Linked: qulCIGxnTUs (LinkedIn, 11 min, human captions, Presentations shelf) — see shadow.why for what it models and what it does not. Runners-up: jziHvsed5h4 ('Stop Freezing When Your Manager Questions You in Meetings', Linda Raynier, 21 min, auto captions) is the best lesson on the behaviour itself — 'conclusion first, then the thinking… the most executive style communication… senior leaders tend to lead with the so what', 'one reason, maybe two at most', and a directed next step ('Do you want me to pull two options together and bring them back by Thursday?') — but it teaches contributing in a meeting rather than giving an update, and its captions are automatic; 7AS94R-7YCs ('How to Get People to Listen to You', HBR, 10 min, human) says 'get to the point' and 'bottom line' about being heard, not about summarising; 5KjQV3GNG6s ('Know Before You Tell', Think Fast Talk Smart, 24 min, auto) is a conversation about the rule of three; -tubDR5XSRw (Week 2's clip) is about organising one idea, not a leadership summary. The 'headline' caption hits in the BBC news-vocabulary clips (8ip3fMwdhx0, K8Dwy0u5pp8, zl0dwwKhmuM, FuExlxdoTcY, ScyumiPXca8) are newspaper headlines; 'executive' in the Stanford and HBR clips is the job title. The curriculum's Monday task ('Shadow an executive update / business presentation clip') is met by the linked clip, which is that genre; what the library lacks is the Tuesday and Thursday turn itself: no clip is a manager giving a 60-second project summary to a leader with a named risk and a decision asked for — that is a content-library gap, and a reviewer can relink here when one is added.

moves.label: Lead with the headline
moves.hint: The conclusion first, in one line, before any detail — the sentence a leader would repeat if they left the room now.
patterns: The headline is: the rollout is on track for the 30th, with one thing still open.
The short version: 260 of the 400 thousand is contracted, and the rest depends on one supplier.
In one sentence: the system works, and the risk is the date, not the software.
moves.retry: Say it again and open with the headline — "the headline is…", "the short version…", "in one sentence…" — the conclusion before any detail.
cues: what you need to know is
if you only hear one thing
moves._cue_note: A headline is the conclusion said first, and announced as such: 'the headline is…', 'the short version…', 'in one sentence…', 'the key message…'. 'Let me give you a summary' or 'quick update' promises one and proves nothing; a bare status ('we're on track', Week 2 and Week 8) is not a headline unless it is framed as the message; the bare word 'headline' in a list of words is not credited, so the cues carry the frame ('the headline', 'headline is'). 'Bottom line' is the close (the land move), never the headline, and 'the story is' is left out because Week 8 learners say 'the checkout story is blocked'.

moves.label: Signpost the shape
moves.hint: Tell the listener how to listen — how many things are coming, or that you'll be brief — before the first one.
patterns: Three things to know.
At a high level, two of the three regions are live and the third is due on the 30th.
I'll keep it brief: the numbers first, then what could slip, then what I need.
moves.retry: Say it again and tell the listener the shape before the detail — "three things to know", "at a high level", "I'll keep it brief", "the first thing… the second…".
moves._cue_note: A signpost announces the shape — 'three things to know', 'at a high level', 'I'll keep it brief', an enumeration — before the content. 'It's important to be brief' talks about brevity and proves nothing, so 'to be brief' is not a cue and 'I'll be brief' is; 'two of three steps done' is Week 8's status, not a count of points, so '… of three' is never a cue; a bare 'first' or 'high' is too common to count, so the enumeration cues carry their punctuation or their noun and the punctuation-free forms are 'the first thing', 'the second is', 'secondly'. A signpost on its own never passes: it is the frame, not the content.

moves.label: Name the main risk
moves.hint: One risk, named as the main one, with what it would cost — not a list of worries.
patterns: The main risk is the ticket migration: the first dry run took nine hours against a six-hour window.
The biggest risk is the largest supplier — 110 of the 400 thousand sit with them.
The one risk to watch is the December peak: if the date slips, we hit it on the old system.
moves.retry: Say it again and name one risk as the main one — "the main risk is…", "the biggest risk is…", "the one risk to watch…" — with what it would cost.
moves._cue_note: A risk is named as THE risk — main, biggest, key, the one to watch — with what it would cost. 'There are some risks', 'I have a concern' (Week 7's acknowledge/disagree frame), 'that puts the demo at risk' (Week 8's impact) and 'the risk of moving too quickly' (Week 7's reason) are not this move: they describe consequences or worries without ranking one risk above the rest. A date or a deadline is never a risk on its own.

moves.label: Say the decision you need
moves.hint: Name the one decision, who makes it and by when — not a hint that something needs deciding.
patterns: The next decision we need is yours: approve a second dry run this Sunday, or move go-live to the 7th.
The decision I need from you this week is whether we accept 60-day terms to close the third supplier.
So the ask is a decision by Friday: hold the date, or slip a week.
moves.retry: Say it again and name the decision — "the next decision we need is…", "I need a decision on…", "the ask is…" — who makes it and by when.
moves._cue_note: The decision is named as a decision, with an owner: 'the next decision we need is…', 'I need a decision on… by…', 'the ask is…', 'it's your call'. 'We need to decide soon' and 'we should talk about it' prove nothing. 'The recommendation is…' is in the Week 9 phrase bank but is Week 6's move (recommend-decide) and is deliberately not a cue here — a recommendation is what you propose, a decision is what you ask for. 'Could you approve…' and 'sign off' are Week 3's ask and are left out too, so that a Week 3 answer earns nothing here.

moves.label: Land the bottom line
moves.hint: Close with the takeaway in one line — the last thing they hear is the thing to remember.
patterns: Bottom line: we're on track for the 30th if the dry run is approved this week.
The key takeaway is that the target is reachable by quarter-end only with that decision.
In short: the system works, the date is the risk, and the call is yours.
moves.retry: Say it again and close with the takeaway — "bottom line…", "the key takeaway is…", "in short…" — one line they can repeat.
cues: the one thing to take away
moves._cue_note: The close is announced as the takeaway — 'bottom line', 'the key takeaway is', 'in short', 'to sum up'. It is not a headline (that is the first line, not the last) and not a status: 'we're on track' proves nothing without the frame, and Week 5's 'the one thing to remember' is left out because it is that competency's check. 'So the message is' would contain the headline cue 'the message is' and is left out; 'overall' and 'to close' are too common to count.

expressions.def: say the conclusion first, and say that it is the conclusion
open an executive summary — the shape before the detail
tell the listener how many things are coming
signal respect for their time — then keep it
surface the top risk, one, ranked above the rest

expressions.w: the next decision we need is
expressions.def: drive the decision — name it, and who makes it
land the message in one line they can repeat
close with confidence — the takeaway, last

see.where: Tuesday, 4:55 pm. The operations director is between meetings and stops you in the corridor. You run the support-platform rollout — three regions, six months of work — and they have sixty seconds.
see.who: The operations director, who sponsors the rollout and approves overtime
see.asks: Give me the 60-second version.
see.goal: Don't start at the beginning. In about a minute: lead with the headline, signpost the shape, name the main risk, say the decision you need, and land the bottom line.

hear.model: I'll keep it brief. The headline is: the support platform is on track for France on the 30th, and I need one decision from you today. Three things to know. One, the UK and Ireland are live and stable — no open incidents since July. Two, the French agents are all trained, so the people side is done. Three, the main risk is the ticket migration: 150,000 tickets have to move in one weekend, and the first dry run took nine hours against a six-hour window. The engineers have a fix and want a second dry run this Sunday. The next decision we need is yours: approve weekend overtime for two engineers for that dry run. If it fits the window, we go live on the 30th; if not, we move to the 7th. Bottom line: on track for the 30th, one approval needed today.
hear.note: Five moves in about 140 words — a minute at speaking pace. The headline is the conclusion, said first; 'three things' tells the listener how to listen; one risk is named as the main one, with what it would cost; the decision is named, with who makes it and by when; the last line is the one they can repeat in their next meeting.

missions.prompt: Give me the 60-second version.
missions.context: The new customer-support platform is rolling out to three regions. The UK and Ireland went live in June and July and have had no open incidents since July. France is due to go live on the 30th, and all the French agents are trained. The main risk is the ticket migration: 150,000 French tickets have to move over one weekend, and the first dry run took nine hours against a six-hour window. The engineers have a fix and want a second dry run this Sunday, which needs the director's approval for weekend overtime for two engineers. If the second run fits the window, go-live stays on the 30th; if not, it moves to the 7th. Nobody has asked the director yet.

see.where: Steering committee, Thursday. The CFO joins for ten minutes, has not read the pack, and turns to you about the supplier-consolidation programme. No slides; you have about three minutes.
see.who: The CFO, who owns the savings target and can change payment terms
see.asks: I haven't read the pack — what do I need to know?
see.goal: Nobody is prompting you this time. Lead with the headline, signpost the shape, name the main risk, say the decision you need from the CFO, and land the bottom line — in three minutes, not thirty.

missions.prompt: I haven't read the pack — what do I need to know?
missions.context: The programme's savings target is 400 thousand this financial year. Contracts are signed with two of the four suppliers, worth 260 thousand. The fourth supplier is on schedule to sign next month for 60 thousand. The third supplier is the largest — 110 thousand of the target — and that negotiation has stalled for three weeks on payment terms: they want 60 days, the company standard is 45. Finance can accept 60 days if the CFO agrees; nobody has asked yet, and the supplier's offer lapses on Friday. Without the third supplier the year lands at 320 thousand, short of the target; with it, the target is met.

competencies.title: Interview & networking communication
competencies.objective: Stop reciting your duties when someone asks about your experience: set the scene, claim your part, say what you actually did, give the result with a number, and say what it taught you — so an interviewer or a new contact remembers one story with your name on it, not a job description.

shadow.title: English Job Interview Tips and Tricks 2 - How to Answer Job Interview Questions in English
shadow.why: A Business English lesson with human captions, on the Interviews shelf: a podcast host explaining how to answer interview questions about what you have done, with two worked answers. It teaches the exact shape of this competency — 'keep it to three simple parts: the situation, what you did, and the result' — and models it twice ('just last month we had a big project with a demanding client, and three developers got sick… So I managed to flex some other projects and transfer some staff. In the end, we had good outcomes and happy clients'). It also teaches two of the week's habits: link an achievement to the bigger picture, and 'give credit where credit is due'. It models three of the five moves clearly — the scene, the action and the result — and the ownership only loosely, because the speaker acts in the first person but never claims the task as his; its results are 'good outcomes and happy clients', never a number, and it draws no lesson from either story. So it is the Monday interview clip and a model of the story's shape, not of the whole turn.

competencies._shadow_note: Linked after a content check of the 301-clip catalogue (315 caption files, 2026-09-23). Titles and captions were scanned for interview, networking, career, hiring, achievement, 'tell me about a time', 'tell me about yourself', STAR, situation / task / action / result, ownership, 'what I learned' and the ten Week 10 phrases. The catalogue has an Interviews shelf of seven clips and three networking clips, so the choice was made on captions, not titles. Linked: xk5rp4qCU8M (Business English Pod, 7.6 min, human captions with word times, Interviews shelf) — see shadow.why for what it models and what it does not. Runners-up: vC4wlYS2bkY ('AI Interview Tips: What to Expect & How to Pass', Indeed, 4 min, human) has the library's best single answer — 'Last year, my team had three product deadlines land in the same week. I was responsible for coordinating resources… As a result, we launched on time, and adoption rose by 18%' — ownership, action and a quantified result in four sentences, but the clip is about being screened by a machine and the rest of it is set-up advice; GDBH3-JAFk8 ('Nursing Interview Questions', Indeed, human) and fBxDwJHeHcE ('Administrative Assistant Interview Questions', Indeed, human) both name the STAR method and say 'a great story shows impact, not effort… what changed because of you', but their sample answers are written for one profession; OGU7BeJ5bEs and AKUxbgjR9sg (the same podcast's parts 3 and 1) cover 'where do you see yourself' and preparation, not the story; 06umbgKFr2c ('You Have 30 Seconds', Indeed, 10 min) is the elevator pitch and 'tell me about yourself', which is Week 1's ground; RMnJfjfsFDE and SzIs-aVk8dE (Linda Raynier, auto captions) are about interview mindset; wyzjEP3Ku7I ('CRUSH Your Next Interview!', Rachel's English, 25 min) is a pronunciation drill on interview sentences; the three networking clips (6Qukx9ESyxI, E0OaadAGTWY, z43_IaKJfWo) are about how to network, and -ddNt8yWjIY ('The Networking Elevator') is a listening-comprehension dialogue — none of them a story about experience. The curriculum's Monday task ('Shadow an interview or professional networking conversation clip') is met by the linked clip, which is an interview lesson with modelled answers rather than a recorded interview; what the library lacks is a real candidate telling one story with a number and a lesson in it — that is a content-library gap, and a reviewer can relink here when one is added.

moves.label: Set the scene
moves.hint: The situation you walked into, in one or two lines — the problem, the numbers, the stakes — before anything about you.
patterns: The situation was that refunds were taking nineteen days on average, and refund complaints were the biggest category in our customer survey.
The challenge was a forty-person field team spending nearly three hours a day driving between jobs.
When I joined, the monthly report was two weeks late every month and nobody could say why.
moves.retry: Say it again and open with the scene — "the situation was…", "the challenge was…", "when I joined…" — the problem and the numbers before anything about you.
moves._cue_note: The scene is a past problem with its stakes, framed as the story's starting point: 'the situation was…', 'the challenge was…', 'when I joined…', 'in my last role…'. Week 3's 'there's a problem with…' and 'the problem is…' are a live issue being raised now, not a story, so only the past forms are cues ('the problem was that', 'there was a problem'); Week 2's and Week 8's status ('we're behind', 'on track') and Week 1's 'at the moment' are the present and are left out; 'it started when' is Week 3's cause and is not a cue. A bare date ('in 2024') or a bare 'last year' is not a scene, so the time cues carry a subject ('last year we', 'last year I'). A scene on its own never passes: it is the set-up, not the evidence.

moves.label: Claim your part
moves.hint: What was yours in it — led, owned, was asked to — said in the first person, not 'we'.
patterns: Nobody owned the whole process, so I took ownership of it end to end.
I led the effort to fix the routing.
It was my job to get the three teams to agree on one set of numbers.
moves.retry: Say it again and claim your part in the first person — "I led the effort to…", "I took ownership of…", "it was my job to…" — what was yours, not what the team did.
moves._cue_note: Ownership is claimed in the first person and in the past: 'I led the effort to…', 'I took ownership of…', 'I was asked to…', 'it fell to me'. Week 1's 'I'm responsible for' and 'I look after' describe today's job, not a story, so only the past forms count ('I was responsible for'); 'we led', 'we owned' and 'the team took it on' credit the team and prove nothing about the speaker; 'I was involved in' and 'I helped with' are participation, not ownership, and are not cues. 'I managed to…' is an outcome, not a role, and is left out.

moves.label: Say what you did
moves.hint: The concrete steps you took — mapped, set up, persuaded, brought together — and who you did them with.
patterns: The first thing I did was map every step with one person from each team.
I got finance to agree to refund low-value items on receipt, and I set up a weekly fifteen-minute call between the three teams.
I collaborated with the dispatchers to try zone-based scheduling in one region for six weeks.
moves.retry: Say it again and give the steps — "the first thing I did was…", "I set up…", "I collaborated with…", "I influenced the decision by…" — what you actually did, and with whom.
moves._cue_note: An action is a concrete step in the first person: 'the first thing I did was…', 'I set up…', 'I persuaded…', 'I collaborated with…'. 'We changed the process' hides the speaker; 'I was responsible for changing it' is the ownership move, not a step; 'so I' and 'then I' are too common to count, so every cue carries a verb. Week 1's 'I work closely with' is the present and is not a cue; Week 3's 'I've already spoken to' is a mitigation being reported now, not a story, and is left out. 'I ran the project' belongs to ownership, so no action cue starts 'I ran'.

moves.label: Give the result
moves.hint: What changed, with a number — from what to what, by how much, by when.
patterns: The result was that the average refund time fell from nineteen days to six within four months.
As a result we launched on time, and refund complaints dropped by about sixty per cent.
Overtime came back within budget, and it's now rolled out to all four regions.
moves.retry: Say it again and give the result with a number — "the result was…", "as a result…", "we went from… to…", "it fell from… to…" — what changed, by how much.
moves._cue_note: The result is announced as the outcome, in the past, and carries a change: 'the result was…', 'as a result…', 'went from… to…', 'fell from… to…', 'within budget'. Week 1's 'the result is' and 'which saves' are the purpose of a job today, not what a story achieved, so only the past forms count; Week 2's 'this means…' and Week 8's 'at risk' are impact, not result; Week 5's 'you no longer' is a benefit and is left out. 'It went well' and 'it was a success' prove nothing, and a percentage in the scene ('thirty per cent over budget') is the problem, not the result, so a bare 'per cent' is not a cue. 'Fell to' is left out because 'it fell to me' is the ownership move.

moves.label: Say what it taught you
moves.hint: One line of reflection that points forward — what you learned, and the work you want more of.
patterns: What I learned from that was that when a problem crosses teams, someone has to hold the whole picture.
That experience taught me that I do my best work where data and persuasion meet.
It's why I'm looking to grow into a role where that is the whole job.
moves.retry: Say it again and close with the lesson — "what I learned from that was…", "that experience taught me…", "I'm looking to grow into…" — one line that points forward.
cues: i would like to grow into
why i want to move into
the role i am looking for
moves._cue_note: The lesson is named as a lesson and points forward: 'what I learned from that was…', 'that experience taught me…', 'it's why I'm looking to grow into…'. 'I learned a lot' is enthusiasm without content and is not a cue, so the cues carry a continuation ('I learned that', 'I learned to'); Week 9's 'the takeaway is' and 'bottom line' are a summary's close, not a reflection, and are left out; Week 6's 'the next step is' is a plan, not growth, so no cue contains 'next step'. A lesson on its own never passes: it is the close of a story that has to have been told.

expressions.def: open the story with the problem, before anything about you
claim the lead, in the first person
say it was yours — accountability, not participation
a step you took with others — the teamwork inside the story
leadership without authority — how you moved the decision
announce the outcome, then give the number

expressions.w: what I learned from that was
expressions.def: show growth — the lesson, in one line

see.where: Thursday, 10:15. Second-round interview for a senior coordinator role at an online furniture retailer. The hiring manager has your CV on the table, the small talk is over, and they have twenty minutes for the real questions.

moves.label: Name what's at stake for them
moves.hint: Open on the thing THIS listener owns — their target, their budget, their priority — not on your problem.
patterns: What's at stake here is your pricing launch: it lands on a catalogue that is wrong one time in nine.
The thing you care about is output per shift, and that is exactly what this is costing.
You've said the priority this half is the renewal, and this is the thing most likely to lose it.

moves._cue_note: The stake is the LISTENER'S: their target, their budget, their priority, the thing they are measured on, named as what this decides. Week 5's 'what this means for you' and 'the impact on you' are that competency's check and are deliberately not cues here, and neither is 'the benefit is' or 'the value is'. Week 2's, Week 3's and Week 8's bare 'at risk' is an impact statement about a date and is never this move, so no cue contains 'at risk' — 'at stake' is the frame that carries the listener. Week 9's 'the main risk is' ranks a risk in an update and is left out too. A stake on its own never passes: it is the frame, not the case.

moves.label: Give the cost of doing nothing
moves.hint: What carrying on as we are costs — a number, a rate, or what it has already cost.

Every month we wait costs us two more mispriced orders a day.
moves.retry: Say it again and cost the inaction — "the cost of delay is…", "if we ignore this…", "every month we wait…" — what doing nothing costs, with a number.
moves._cue_note: This is the price of NOT acting, said as such: 'the cost of delay is…', 'if we ignore this…', 'every month we wait…', 'it's costing us…'. Week 6's 'the trade-off is' and 'the cost of that' are what the recommended option costs — the opposite direction — and are not cues. Week 2's and Week 3's 'this means Friday is at risk' and 'cost us a week' are the impact of a problem on a date, so 'cost us' in the past never counts and only the present 'it's costing us' does. Week 9's 'the main risk is' ranks a risk rather than pricing inaction. A consequence with no cost in it ('it would be bad') proves nothing.

moves.label: Back it with evidence

I'm confident because we have six months of data on that line, not a hunch.
moves.retry: Say it again and show where the numbers came from — "the data supports…", "we audited…", "I'm confident because…" — evidence, not opinion.
moves._cue_note: Evidence is the provenance of the numbers: 'the data supports', 'we audited', 'the log shows', 'I'm confident because'. Week 6's and Week 7's 'the data shows', 'the numbers show', 'the evidence is' and 'based on' justify a choice between options and are deliberately left out, so this move cannot be earned by a Week 6 answer. Week 10's 'I measured', 'I tracked' and 'I tested' are steps inside a past story and are not cues; the plural forms used here are about the case in front of the listener. 'I think', 'obviously' and 'everyone knows' are the opposite of this move.

moves._cue_note: The return is what the ask buys back, as a payback or a recovered number: 'pays for itself within', 'the return on', 'it buys us', 'frees up'. competencies.title: Final integration week
competencies.objective: Put the twelve weeks together in one turn: give the status, ask the question that clears the ambiguity, say where you differ, recommend one way forward, and close with the bottom line — under time pressure, in front of people who each want something different.
competencies.pattern: UPDATE → CLARIFY → PUSH BACK → RECOMMEND → SUMMARISE
competencies._integration_note: Week 12 is an INTEGRATION competency, not a twelfth communication behaviour. weeks.json calls it 'Final integration week' with the goal 'Combine everything under realistic pressure', its Thursday task is 'Full contribution: update → clarification → disagreement → recommendation → summary', and every phrase in its own 'Integration' bank is labelled a chain of earlier weeks ('Chain: summary → issue → recommendation', 'Chain: pushback → persuasion'). So it invents no new frames: each of the five moves is an earlier competency's beat, reused, and `integrates` records which. THE EVIDENCE RULE, which is the whole point: a Week 12 attempt writes evidence ONLY to the final-integration record. It writes nothing to clear-update, clarify-confirm, disagree-pushback, recommend-decide or exec-summary — not an attempt, and not a support row. Doing either would be mastery inflation: chaining a behaviour once inside a five-part turn under time pressure is not the same as demonstrating that competency on its own mission, and the engine's own rule is that only a recorded answer to a competency's mission is evidence for it. The support array was considered and rejected on top of that: supportSummary derives bestRung/rungName from SHADOW_RUNGS and the evidence screen renders 'Shadowed this clip N× — furthest step reached…' whenever support.total > 0, so an integration row there would make the app claim Shadow work the learner never did. Nothing is lost by the decision, because the Week 12 attempt's own moves map already records exactly which underlying behaviours appeared, and the weakest of them drives the retry, the coach line and the next recommendation through the ordinary engine.
